title: A Reproducible Synthetic Benchmark and Deterministic Validator for Evaluating LLM‑Driven NetOps: A Paired Confirmatory Comparison of a GVR Pipeline and Single‑Pass Generation
abstract: We designed, preregistered, and executed a sealed, machine‑checkable synthetic benchmark and deterministic validator to compare a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline against a frozen single‑pass LLM on operational intent→configuration tasks. The preregistered paired design used N=300 tasks across four intent categories (75 per cluster) and declared model gpt-5-mini; validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0). The study applied a shared‑initial generation: baseline and guarded conditions received the same initial candidate; the guarded pipeline could invoke repair only if the deterministic validator failed (maximum one repair call per task). Provider accounting shows 300 shared initial generation calls and exactly one repair invocation (total model calls used = 301). Results: baseline 299/300 passes, guarded 300/300 passes; contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0033333333333332993; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The preregistered hypothesis that GVR produces a materially higher pass rate (target effect 0.10 at ≈80% power with N=300) was not supported. We analyse reasons (ceiling effect, minimal GVR engagement), report complete execution accounting, and provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for benchmark design. All preregistration, execution, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived for community reuse.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and automated remediation. Prior work demonstrates both promise and risk: LLMs can draft device configurations but produce syntax, topology, or semantic errors unless combined with verification and human oversight. The NetOps community lacks standardized, machine‑checkable benchmarks that couple operational intent tasks with deterministic validator semantics and sealed preregistration to support confirmatory comparisons of defended pipelines (generate–validate–repair, GVR) versus single‑pass generation.

This work reports a sealed, preregistered, machine‑checkable experiment (study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1) that (1) constructs a synthetic intent→configuration task bank, (2) implements a deterministic snapshot validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, v5.0) with explicit intent constraints, and (3) runs a preregistered paired comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline against a frozen single‑pass generator (declared model gpt-5-mini). The study intentionally used a shared‑initial generation: baseline and guarded conditions initially received the same generated candidate so that any guarded improvement must derive from an invoked repair. Our primary confirmatory question was: under fixed seeds and a constrained repair budget (≤1 repair call per task), does GVR materially increase the per‑task validator pass rate relative to a frozen single‑pass LLM?
sections.related_work: Surveys and focused technical studies report accelerated interest in LLMs for NetOps and highlight persistent evaluation, realism, and safety gaps (e.g., comprehensive surveys and NetOps reviews). Prior experimental work shows that verifier‑assisted and repair‑oriented architectures can reduce misconfigurations in limited settings but generally rely on human adjudication or small testbeds. Research on intent→configuration translation and verifier‑assisted prompting (generate–validate–repair) reports improved correctness under specific datasets and workflows. Complementary literature documents prompt injection, jailbreaks, hallucination, and adversarial attacks as concrete operational risks for LLM‑driven automation. Collectively, this prior work motivates a sealed, artifact‑grounded confirmatory comparison that fixes generator variance via a shared‑initial design and isolates repair efficacy under a constrained budget.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration. We preregistered study ac-2026-003-prereg-v1 before execution. Primary hypothesis H1: the GVR pipeline yields a higher per‑task validator pass rate than a frozen single‑pass generator on N=300 paired tasks (two‑sided α=0.05). The preregistration specifies the task bank, validator semantics, model and adapter configuration, sampling budget, exclusion rules, missingness treatment, and the exact analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1).

Task bank and semantics. The deterministic task generator produced N=300 synthetic intent→configuration tasks partitioned into four intent clusters (reachability, isolation, ACLs, route policies; 75 tasks each). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, allowed_fields, workflow_policies, and an explicit required_sequence of field changes necessary to satisfy the intent. Tasks span device counts 3–50 and abstract multi‑vendor device models; they are synthetic and contain no private customer data.

Validator and scoring. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version v5.0) implements the scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation. The validator accepts a configuration candidate if and only if all declared constraints and required sequences are satisfied in a snapshot semantics: field changes and final states are checked against the expected_final_state and workflow_policies; violations are enumerated and returned. The validator is deterministic and stateless (snapshot check), intentionally conservative to yield binary pass/fail outcomes per task.

Experimental design and shared‑initial semantics. The paired design used a single shared initial generation per task: the pipeline issued one generation call yielding the shared candidate, which served as the baseline single‑pass output. For the guarded condition the pipeline ran the deterministic validator on the same shared candidate and, only if the validator reported failure, was it permitted up to one automated repair call (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). This design tightly controls generator variance: improvements attributed to the guarded condition must arise from repair rather than different initial samples. The preregistration defined planned_episode_count = 600 (300 shared initial + up to 300 repairs) and required ≥270 completed pairs to support confirmatory inference.

Model and runtime configuration. The declared model and runtime configuration in the hosted adapter were: declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"; requested_model = "gpt-5-mini"; provider = "openai_responses"; max_output_tokens = 2000; maximum_attempts_per_call = 1; reasoning_effort = "minimal"; store = false; temperature = null. The hosted adapter operated in a deterministic sampling mode so that shared initial generation outputs were repeatable under the recorded provider conditions. Exact provider call traces for every model call (including the single repair call) are archived in the execution bundle.

Analysis plan. The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed on N=300 paired binary outcomes. The preregistered test was exact McNemar two‑sided; a paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval was computed with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Sensitivity treatments for missingness and exclusion rules were preregistered; no exclusions or missing pairs occurred in the run.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. Execution completed per preregistration: planned_episode_count = 600, completed_episode_count = 600, complete_pair_count = 300, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 301. Provider_call_audit recorded stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1} and condition_counts = {shared: 300, guarded: 1}; therefore the guarded repair stage executed exactly once under the preregistered repair budget. All per‑call provider traces and validator diagnostics are archived in the execution bundle.

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Aggregated counts are: baseline_success_count = 299/300 (baseline_success_rate = 0.9966666666666667); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table (guarded vs baseline) is: n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333333333332993. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729): [0.00, 0.01]. Table 1 (below) displays these counts and summary statistics.

Interpretation and diagnostics. Two instrumentally documented facts explain the null confirmatory outcome. First, a near‑ceiling baseline (299/300) leaves almost no room for the preregistered detectable paired effect (0.10). The power calculation in the preregistration assumed baseline rates substantially lower than observed; with baseline ≈0.997 a 0.10 absolute improvement is impossible. Second, the guarded pipeline rarely differed from baseline because the validator accepted the shared candidate in almost all tasks; the guarded repair stage invoked only once. Consequently, the paired test compared identical shared candidates in the vast majority of pairs rather than repaired alternatives, and the one discordant outcome (n10=1) is insufficient to reject equality in an exact two‑sided McNemar enumeration. The single repair invocation and its provider trace are archived in the execution bundle and indexed in the execution manifest and raw results for auditors and reproducers.

Representative examples. The archived bundle contains per‑task scoring JSONs and shared initial responses for representative tasks (e.g., task-000001 … task-000006). Those examples illustrate validator traces (normalized_configuration, required_command_count, final_state) and show that many tasks required multi‑step sequences (e.g., shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change). In the archived artifacts the difference between normalization and canonical reference answers is visible and deterministic validator outputs (VALID_CONFIGURATION or enumerated violation codes) are provided for each candidate.

Power and sensitivity post‑hoc. The preregistered power routine targeted detection of a 0.10 paired improvement at ≈80% power with N=300 under conservative discordance assumptions. Observed baseline ≈0.997 violates those assumptions: achievable paired improvement is at most 0.00333 given the observed data. This arithmetic sensitivity observation is computed directly from the observed contingency and the preregistered power routine and explains lack of statistical significance.
sections.discussion:
Null and ceiling‑effect diagnosis. The confirmatory null result is best read as a null result for the specific preregistered question under the chosen task bank, validator semantics, and constrained repair budget. Two closely linked causes produced this outcome: (1) a highly effective generator for this synthetic task bank under the chosen deterministic sampling settings, producing correct shared candidates in 299/300 tasks, and (2) the guarded pipeline's trigger policy limited repair attempts to validator failures and permitted at most one repair call per task; with so few failures the repair subsystem had almost no opportunity to demonstrate benefit. Together these produce a ceiling effect that invalidates the preregistered detectability assumptions.

Operational implications and concrete benchmark recommendations. Artifact‑grounded lessons lead to concrete recommendations for benchmark design when the research goal is to evaluate repair value: (A) raise task difficulty or include adversarial/seeding modes that produce more initial generator failures; (B) permit larger or iterative repair budgets (multiple repair attempts per failed candidate) so that repair can exercise localized fixes; (C) evaluate multiple independent generations per task as baseline samples rather than a single shared candidate, to measure generator variance and the value of repair‑mediated selection; (D) incorporate stateful validators or execution emulation that model in‑flight side effects and temporal ordering rather than purely snapshot checks. Each recommendation directly follows from execution accounting (300 shared initial generations, a single repair invocation) and the per‑task validator diagnostics archived in the execution bundle.

Reproducibility, determinism, and limitations. The hosted adapter used deterministic sampling settings (temperature unset/adapter deterministic mode) to ensure repeatable shared‑initial outputs under the same provider conditions. Bit‑for‑bit reproduction therefore requires (a) access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in the archived model configuration and provider call traces, and (b) replay of the archived per‑call provider traces. The archived execution bundle contains the raw_results index, the per‑call provider traces, and the model configuration used for the run; reproducers should use those artifacts as authoritative references. We note external validity limits: tasks are synthetic (abstracted device models, snapshot validator), only one declared model (gpt-5-mini) and one deterministic validator were evaluated, and the snapshot validator intentionally omits vendor execution idiosyncrasies and runtime temporal dynamics.

Failure‑mode analysis and future work. Only one discordant pair (n10=1) occurred, which leaves planned exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered. However, the archived per‑task diagnostics enable future community meta‑analysis: researchers can extract failure patterns, compute difficulty stratified error rates, seed adversarial candidates, or instrument more aggressive repair policies. We release the full execution manifest and per‑call traces so the community can pursue these follow‑on investigations without reconstructing our pipeline.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and archived a sealed synthetic NetOps benchmark and deterministic validator and ran a paired confirmatory comparison of a guarded GVR pipeline versus a frozen single‑pass gpt-5-mini generator on N=300 intent→configuration tasks. Both approaches achieved near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300; guarded 300/300). The preregistered hypothesis that GVR materially improves pass rate (target 0.10) was not supported on this task set. The run's provider accounting shows the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks, so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about the general effectiveness of automatic repair. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, raw responses, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts so the community can extend this benchmark with harder tasks, iterative repair budgets, and multi‑model comparisons to better evaluate when GVR pipelines provide measurable operational value.

Orchestration/adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 implemented the shared initial generation (single shared call per task) and the guarded generate–validate–repair pipeline with maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. No manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces snapshot intent constraints but does not model temporal in‑flight execution dynamics, vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, or asynchronous side effects.

External validity: tasks are synthetic (device counts 3–50, abstracted multi‑vendor models) and may not capture production heterogeneity; findings do not imply equivalent performance on real production networks or private customer data.

Ceiling effect: near‑perfect pass rates (baseline 299/300, guarded 300/300) reduce sensitivity to detect the preregistered target effect (0.10) and therefore constrain confirmatory inference about practical superiority of GVR under broader conditions.
Model and scope limits: only gpt-5-mini was declared and evaluated; findings do not generalize to other model families or sizes without further experiments.

GVR engagement: the guarded repair stage executed only once across N=300 tasks (provider recorded stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=1), so the guarded condition rarely differed from baseline; this pipeline inactivity constrains conclusions about repair effectiveness under alternative trigger policies or larger repair budgets.
Failure‑mode analysis: only one discordant outcome occurred (n10=1), leaving exploratory failure clustering and subgroup inference underpowered and inconclusive.

Reproducibility caveat: reproducing identical hosted model outputs may require access to the same hosted model release and provider invocation semantics recorded in the archived model configuration and the per‑call provider traces archived in the execution bundle.

Artifact‑inclusion note: the exact per‑task artifacts that contain the single repair provider trace and the single discordant episode identifier are present in the archived execution bundle (execution manifest and raw_results) and are authoritative for auditors.
